notes:
I've written notes for every verse, though some get only one or two points. Many of the "traditional reading" notes come from David Guzik (Enduring Word / Blue Letter Bible), with other material from Precept Austin, Bible Hub and StudyLight.

**What I couldn't find:**
- **Missing views:** nothing from bibleodyssey.org, NET Bible notes or any Orthodox site; no Methodist/Wesleyan source; and no prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace reading of this chapter.
- **Lutheran:** the only Lutheran voice is Lenski on v. 7.
- **Mary and Jesus' brothers (v. 14):** I found no Catholic or Orthodox page on this verse.
- **Unread pages:** the Precept Austin chapter page broke off partway through v. 1, and the Blue Letter Bible page didn't load. Where I quote Guzik on vv. 3–26, I'm using the search snippet from his Blue Letter Bible study guide, which is cut off partway through v. 26.

---

**v. 1**
- The "first book" is Luke's Gospel. The word "began" means the Gospel covers only the start of Jesus' work; Acts shows it continuing, and it still continues today. (Guzik) https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-1/
- Guzik also gives three options for Theophilus: a Christian wanting teaching, a Roman official being briefed, or a symbolic name meaning "God‑lover." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-1/
- Griffith‑Thomas notes that "doing" comes before "teaching." The "doing" comes first, for Christianity is primarily life. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-of-the-apostles-outline-studies-in-primitive-christianity
- Stott suggests a fuller title for the book: something like "The Continuing Words and Deeds of Jesus by His Spirit through His Apostles." https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-1-commentary

**v. 2**
- Even as the risen Lord, Jesus gave his instructions "through the Holy Spirit." Guzik says that if Jesus relied on the Spirit, so should we. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-1/
- Precept Austin also points to Jesus' dependence on the Spirit as an example for us to follow. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts_18_commentary

**v. 3**
- The "convincing proofs" left no doubt that Jesus had risen. Guzik links them to the 500 witnesses of 1 Corinthians 15:6. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-1/
- Guzik rejects Gnostic and New Age claims that Jesus taught secret doctrines during the 40 days. Luke reminds us that Jesus simply taught them much the same material that He had taught them in His earthly ministry. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/guzik_david/StudyGuide_Act/Act_1.cfm

**v. 4**
- Jesus has nothing else for the disciples to do other than to wait for the coming of the Holy Spirit. He knows that they really can do nothing effective for the Kingdom of God until the Spirit comes. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/guzik_david/StudyGuide_Act/Act_1.cfm
- Guzik sees the Trinity here: Jesus speaks of the Father's promise, which is the Holy Spirit. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/guzik_david/StudyGuide_Act/Act_1.cfm

**v. 5: Traditional reading**
- Ellicott: their spirits would be plunged into the Spirit's power just as their bodies had been plunged into the Jordan. He says the exact day was left open to train their faith and patience. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/1-5.htm
- Jamieson‑Fausset‑Brown and Poole agree: it was ten days later, but no date was given so they would watch every day. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/1-5.htm
- Gill: baptising with the Spirit is Christ's own right. He quotes Cyril of Jerusalem's picture of being surrounded on every side, like someone under water. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/1-5.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary asks when the apostles themselves were baptised. It suggests Pentecost was the complement of that baptism, not the substitute for it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/1-5.htm

**v. 5: Where traditions differ (when Spirit baptism happens)**
- *Spirit baptism happens at conversion (evangelical / Reformed Baptist):*
  - GotQuestions: Spirit baptism is the work that unites the believer with Christ and his body at the moment of salvation. https://www.gotquestions.org/Spirit-baptism.html
  - John MacArthur (gty.org): The baptism of the Spirit occurs at salvation. He treats the "filling" of Acts 2:4 as something different that comes afterwards. https://www.gty.org/library/sermons-library/1703/the-baptism-of-the-holy-spirit-part-1
  - Don Stewart: Spirit baptism is not a "second blessing" after salvation. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/stewart_don/faq/baptism-with-the-holy-spirit/10-does-the-baptism-with-the-holy-spirit-occur-the-moment-every-person-is-saved.cfm
  - Ray Pritchard: there are not two Holy Spirits, one for "minor" gifts and one for "major" gifts. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/62021/
- *Pentecostal (Assemblies of God):*
  - Luke's opening chapter ties the promised Spirit baptism to power for witness. https://enrichmentjournal.ag.org/Issues/2010/Spring-2010/Baptism-in-the-Holy-Spirit-and-the-Book-of-Acts
  - The same article reads Acts 19:2 as receiving the Spirit "after" believing, followed by tongues. https://enrichmentjournal.ag.org/Issues/2010/Spring-2010/Baptism-in-the-Holy-Spirit-and-the-Book-of-Acts
  - An AG FAQ says the first Spirit baptism is only the beginning of a lifelong experience. https://news.ag.org/en/articles/spiritual-life/2019/05/faq%20baptism%20in%20the%20holy%20spirit
- *A middle view (John Piper, Baptist):*
  - Spirit baptism is an experience of the Spirit given after faith to faith, and a Christian without power is a Christian who needs a baptism in the Holy Spirit. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/how-to-receive-the-gift-of-the-holy-spirit
  - But Piper also says tongues are not necessary for being baptised in the Spirit. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/how-to-receive-the-gift-of-the-holy-spirit
- *Guzik (Calvary Chapel):* it may be better to treat Spirit baptism as a *condition* ("Are you…?") than as a one‑time *experience* ("Have you been…?"). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-1/

**v. 6: Traditional reading and a real divide**
- *Calvin (Reformed), quoted by Guzik:* the question shows the disciples' ignorance. "There are as many errors in this question as words." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/guzik_david/StudyGuide_Act/Act_1.cfm
- *Stott, quoted by Guzik:* the words "restore," "Israel" and "at this time" show they expected a political, national and immediate kingdom. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-1/
- *Guzik:* the question was reasonable given the New Covenant promises, and Jesus did not rebuke them. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-1/
- *Dispensational view (Precept Austin):*
  - Jesus' silence means their perception of a future kingdom was correct. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-1-commentary
  - The Moody Bible Commentary says the church did not fulfil the promises to Israel in their fullest sense. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-1-commentary
  - Donald Grey Barnhouse goes so far as to call amillennialism a great heresy. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-1-commentary
- *Steven Cole:* criticising the disciples for thinking of an earthly kingdom misses the point. The focus should be the Great Commission, not prophetic timetables. https://temp.preceptaustin.org/acts-1-commentary

**v. 7**
- The timing belongs to the Father alone. Jesus did not deny that the kingdom would be restored; he only ruled out guessing at dates. (Guzik) https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/guzik_david/StudyGuide_Act/Act_1.cfm
- *Lenski (Lutheran):* Jesus distinguishes "times" (longer stretches) from "seasons" (shorter, distinct periods). https://temp.preceptaustin.org/acts-1-commentary
- *A. T. Robertson:* people have always been eager to set dates for the second coming. https://temp.preceptaustin.org/acts-1-commentary

**v. 8**
- The Greek "you will be" is a statement of fact, not a command: Jesus was saying they would be witnesses. (Guzik) https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/guzik_david/StudyGuide_Act/Act_1.cfm
- Each place named was unpromising: Jerusalem had executed Jesus, Judea rejected him, Samaritans were despised, and Gentiles were scorned. Yet God wanted witnesses in all of them. (Guzik) https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/guzik_david/StudyGuide_Act/Act_1.cfm
- *Longenecker:* this verse is the theme of the whole book, given as Jesus' last word before the ascension. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-1-commentary
- *J. Vernon McGee:* this is a personal command to every believer, not just to the church as a body. https://temp.preceptaustin.org/acts-1-commentary
- *Stott:* Before Christ sent the church into the world, he sent the Spirit into the church. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/62021/
- "To the end of the earth" uses the same Greek phrase as the Greek Old Testament of Isaiah 49:6. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts_18_commentary

**v. 9**
- Jesus left visibly so the disciples would know he was gone for good, unlike his comings and goings during the 40 days. (Guzik) https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/guzik_david/StudyGuide_Act/Act_1.cfm

**vv. 10–11**
- The two men were apparently angels. They turned the disciples' attention back to obeying Jesus. Jesus told them to go to the ends of the earth, and they stood gazing up into heaven. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/guzik_david/StudyGuide_Act/Act_1.cfm
- Lowell Johnson: the leaving and the return are both personal, visible and physical, and Jesus will return to the same place. https://www.preceptaustin.org/sermons-on-acts-lowell-johnson
- *Catholic:* until the Second Coming of v. 11, Christ appoints visible leaders, the successors of the apostles. https://www.catholic.com/bible-navigator/apostolic-succession/acts120

**v. 12**
- Their obedience stands out. Even with Jesus no longer present, they did exactly what he had said. (Guzik) https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/guzik_david/StudyGuide_Act/Act_1.cfm
- Griffith‑Thomas sets "What was a Sabbath day's journey?" as a study question but doesn't answer it in the part I saw. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-of-the-apostles-outline-studies-in-primitive-christianity

**v. 13**
- Griffith‑Thomas suggests comparing this list of apostles with the lists in the Gospels. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-of-the-apostles-outline-studies-in-primitive-christianity

**v. 14**
- Their unity is striking: the old differences were still there (a tax collector, a Zealot, Peter's denial), but the risen Jesus was greater. (Guzik) https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/guzik_david/StudyGuide_Act/Act_1.cfm
- Jesus' brothers had not supported him before (John 7:5), so their presence here shows the resurrection's power. (Guzik) https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/guzik_david/StudyGuide_Act/Act_1.cfm
- Calvin translates "with the women" as "with their wives," meaning the apostles' wives. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/guzik_david/StudyGuide_Act/Act_1.cfm
- *Protestant comment on Mary (Jack Arnold):* Mary is not a co‑redemptrix. In this context, we find Mary praying to God and not being prayed to. https://temp.preceptaustin.org/acts-1-commentary

**v. 15**
- Peter naturally takes the lead. But Guzik says the idea that Peter's authority was supreme and passed down in unbroken succession is unbiblical and wrong. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/guzik_david/StudyGuide_Act/Act_1.cfm
- GotQuestions agrees that Peter was not the supreme authority over the other apostles. https://www.gotquestions.org/apostolic-succession.html

**vv. 16–17**
- Peter sees that Judas didn't spoil God's plan; he fulfilled it. (Guzik) https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/guzik_david/StudyGuide_Act/Act_1.cfm
- Judas fulfilled prophecy without knowing it and gets no credit for it. Psalm 109:8 shows God planned ahead for the empty place. https://temp.preceptaustin.org/acts-1-commentary

**vv. 18–19**
- *Clarke:* these two verses are probably Luke's own aside, not Peter's words, and should be read in brackets. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/1-18.html
- *Matthew 27 (hanging) and Acts 1 (falling) are usually harmonised:*
  - Barnes says Judas hanged himself, the cord broke, and he fell headlong. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/1-18.html
  - Gill says Matthew tells of the death, while Acts tells what happened to the body afterwards. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/1-18.html
  - I. Howard Marshall suggests the rope broke after the body began to decompose. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/1-18.html
  - Augustine, as quoted by Bible Hub, held the same view. https://biblehub.com/q/Why_does_Acts_differ_on_Judas_death.htm
- *A literary reading (The Gospel Coalition):* Matthew describes how Judas chose to kill himself, while Luke describes the final state of Judas's body. Matthew echoes the death of Absalom; Luke echoes Ahab and focuses on the blood. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/judas-demise-matthew-1-acts-1/
- *Catholic Answers:* the two accounts agree on the timing but describe the death differently. This suggests independent traditions that both confirm Judas died soon after the crucifixion. https://www.catholic.com/audio/ddp/how-judas-iscariot-died
  - It also cites a Papias tradition that Judas survived the hanging and later swelled and burst. https://www.catholic.com/audio/ddp/how-judas-iscariot-died

**v. 20**
- David knew betrayal himself; Doeg betrayed him in 1 Samuel 21–22, and Guzik suggests David may have written these words about Doeg. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/guzik_david/StudyGuide_Act/Act_1.cfm
- *Catholic:* Peter quotes Psalms 69:25 and 109:8 to explain Judas's end and why a successor was needed. https://www.catholic.com/bible-navigator/apostolic-succession/acts120
- Catholic Answers adds that Judas and Matthias could be said to hold a "bishopric." https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/successors-of-the-apostles

**vv. 21–22**
- The requirements came from "sanctified common sense," not a special revelation, and they narrowed the choice to two men. The new apostle's main job was to witness to the resurrection. (Guzik) https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/guzik_david/StudyGuide_Act/Act_1.cfm
- *The debate:*
  - Catholic Answers says the Twelve had to have seen Christ's whole ministry, but a second group of apostles, such as Paul and Barnabas, did not. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/successors-of-the-apostles
  - The Protestant reply, as Catholic Answers presents it, is that the eyewitness requirement can't apply to later "successors." https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/does-christs-church-have-apostolic-succession

**v. 23**
- The name Matthias means "gift of Yahweh." The Catholic Encyclopedia says he was one of the seventy disciples. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/10066a.htm

**vv. 24–25**
- The prayer shows the ascended Lord still in control: he himself chooses Judas's replacement. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/62021/
- On Judas's "own place," Lowell Johnson says it meant a place fitting for him: He went to Hell. https://www.preceptaustin.org/sermons-on-acts-lowell-johnson

**v. 26: Traditional reading and real divides**
- *R. C. Sproul (Reformed):* casting lots followed the Old Testament practice of the Urim and Thummim, leaving the outcome to God's providence. When James was later martyred, he was not replaced. https://learn.ligonier.org/sermons/new-apostle
- *Some say Matthias was the wrong choice and God meant Paul.* Guzik reports this view and begins to answer it with an appeal to Scripture's own testimony, but the snippet cuts off there. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/guzik_david/StudyGuide_Act/Act_1.cfm
- *Catholic:*
  - Matthias was the first apostolic successor. https://www.catholic.com/bible-navigator/apostolic-succession/ephesians219-22
  - Lots were an honoured way of discerning God's will. https://www.catholic.com/bible-navigator/apostolic-succession/acts120
  - One Catholic Answers page also says the apostles laid hands on Matthias. https://www.catholic.com/qa/what-is-the-biblical-support-for-apostolic-succession
- *Evangelical reply (GotQuestions):* Matthias replacing Judas is only an argument for the church replacing an ungodly and unfaithful leader with godly and faithful leaders. https://www.gotquestions.org/apostolic-succession.html
- *Later tradition:* the Catholic Encyclopedia calls the stories of Matthias's later life vague and contradictory. One says he preached in Judea and "Ethiopia" (Colchis) and was crucified. It also notes the critic Zeller judged the election story unhistorical. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/10066a.htm
